name: Base Rate Reasoning
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Why a 99 Percent Accurate Test Can Still Be Wrong More Often Than Right
lesson.summary: Base rate reasoning means weighing how common something is in the first place before trusting a single new piece of evidence about it, and skipping that step is one of the most reliable ways to be fooled by an impressive sounding statistic.
lesson.body:
Earlier in this course you saw that most ambitious technology programs, including quantum computing, fail to deliver on their original timeline. That observation is really an example of a base rate: the underlying frequency of an outcome across many similar cases, measured before you look at any specific new piece of evidence. Base rate reasoning is the general statistical tool behind that observation, and it is one of the most important habits critical thinking can teach you, because people's instincts are naturally drawn to the vividness of whatever evidence is right in front of them (a positive test result, a dramatic demo, a confident headline) while quietly ignoring how common the underlying thing actually was to begin with.

The classic illustration is a medical test. Suppose a disease affects 1 in 100 people in a given population, so its base rate is 1 percent. The screening test for it is genuinely good: it correctly flags 99 percent of people who truly have the disease, and it only misfires on healthy people 5 percent of the time. Now suppose you test positive. Most people's gut reaction is that they almost certainly have the disease, since the test is 99 percent accurate. That gut reaction is wrong, and base rate reasoning shows exactly why.

Picture 10,000 people from this population. About 100 of them, 1 percent, actually have the disease. Of those 100, the test correctly catches 99. The other 9,900 people are healthy, but the test still misfires on 5 percent of them, producing 9,900 times 0.05, which is 495 false positives. So the test produces 99 plus 495, or 594 total positive results, and only 99 of those people actually have the disease. Using Bayes' theorem directly: P(disease given positive) equals P(positive given disease) times P(disease), divided by P(positive), which is (0.99 times 0.01) divided by (0.99 times 0.01 plus 0.05 times 0.99), or 0.0099 divided by 0.0594. That works out to almost exactly 1 in 6, about 16.7 percent. A test described as 99 percent accurate, applied to something rare, leaves you with roughly an 83 percent chance you do not have the disease even after testing positive. The test is not lying. Your intuition about what 99 percent accurate means was the thing that was wrong.

The same math applies to any narrow, rare event claim, including breakthrough announcements in a hard technical field like quantum computing. If genuine, field changing breakthroughs are rare to begin with, and if the announcement system that produces headlines has any nontrivial rate of overstating results, then a dramatic claim needs to be judged not just on how impressive it sounds, but on how rare true breakthroughs actually are and how often the announcement pipeline produces false alarms. The practical habit to build from this chapter is simple: before you react to any new piece of evidence, ask how common this kind of thing actually is. That number becomes your starting point, called a prior, which the next few chapters, on extraordinary claims and on Bayesian reasoning, will show you how to update correctly rather than either ignoring or overriding.
